channels-more.add-line: Add this to the channels list in the connections file, fill in the settings, and save the secrets it names in the default project:
channels-more.docs: How to set this up on their side
channels-more.intro: IRC, Mastodon, Bluesky, iMessage and more, each with its own switch. All of them start off: nothing connects until you switch it on and add it to the connections file.
channels-more.saved: Saved. Connected chat apps follow the new switches now.
channels-more.service.bluesky: Answers Bluesky direct messages sent to the assistant's account; needs its handle and an app password allowed to reach direct messages.
channels-more.service.deltachat: Chat with the assistant on Delta Chat, which carries messages over email; you need the deltachat-rpc-server program installed here with an account already set up.
channels-more.service.discourse: Answers private messages, mentions and replies on a Discourse forum; needs the forum address, the assistant's username and an API key.
channels-more.service.flock: Answers people who write to your Flock app's bot; you need the app secret and the bot token.
channels-more.service.gotify: Sends you a notification through your own Gotify server. Nobody can write back this way.
channels-more.service.guilded: Answers people who mention your Guilded bot in your server's channels; you need the bot's API token.
channels-more.service.homeassistant: Send notifications through a Home Assistant notify service; you need your Home Assistant address and a long-lived access token.
channels-more.service.imessage: Answers iMessages through the Messages app on this Mac. Branch needs Full Disk Access to read new messages and your permission to control Messages; nothing leaves Apple's own service.
channels-more.service.irc: Joins IRC channels under a nick of its own and answers when someone starts a line with that nick, or writes to it privately.
channels-more.service.keybase: Chat with the assistant on Keybase, one to one or in team channels; you need the Keybase app installed on this computer and signed in with the assistant's account.
channels-more.service.mastodon: Answers mentions of the assistant's Mastodon account, privately when they wrote privately; needs the server address and an access token.
channels-more.service.mqtt: Lets devices and scripts on an MQTT broker send the assistant messages and receive its replies; you need the broker's address, the topics to use and, if asked, an account password.
channels-more.service.msteams-bot: Talks in Microsoft Teams as a proper bot, in one-to-one chats, group chats and channels; you need an Azure Bot registration with its app id and a client secret.
channels-more.service.mumble: Answers text messages on a Mumble server, privately or when named in a channel; you need the server's address, a username and, for a self-signed server, its certificate fingerprint.
channels-more.service.nextcloud-talk: Chat with the assistant in Nextcloud Talk conversations; you need your Nextcloud address, a user for the assistant with an app password, and the conversation tokens.
channels-more.service.nostr: Receive and answer encrypted Nostr direct messages through the relays you choose; you need a Nostr private key for the assistant saved as a secret.
channels-more.service.ntfy: Get notifications through ntfy, and optionally write to the assistant on a protected topic; you need the server address, a topic and, for writing back, an access token.
channels-more.service.pumble: Answers direct messages to your Pumble app's bot, and channel messages that mention it; you need the signing secret, the app key, the bot token and the bot's user id.
channels-more.service.pushover: Get notifications on your phone through Pushover; you need an application token and your user key.
channels-more.service.qq-bot: Answers people through an official QQ bot, in private chats, groups and guild channels; you need the bot's App ID and client secret from the QQ open platform.
channels-more.service.reddit: Answers Reddit private messages and username mentions through a script app on the assistant's account; needs the app's id and secret and the account password.
channels-more.service.revolt: Answers direct messages and mentions sent to your Revolt bot; you need the bot's token.
channels-more.service.simplex: Chat with the assistant privately on SimpleX Chat; you need the simplex-chat program running on this computer with its API switched on.
channels-more.service.sms: Text the assistant by SMS through Twilio; you need a Twilio number, the account SID and the auth token.
channels-more.service.synology-chat: Answers people who write to a Chatbot on your Synology NAS; you need the Chatbot's token and its incoming address.
channels-more.service.threema: Send Threema messages through a Threema Gateway ID in Basic mode; you need the Gateway ID, its secret and credits.
channels-more.service.twist: Answers in the Twist conversations you list; needs an access token for the assistant's Twist account and the conversation ids.
channels-more.service.twitch: Reads a Twitch channel's chat and answers when someone mentions the assistant's login. Needs a token from the Twitch developer console.
channels-more.service.vk: Answers messages sent to your VK community through its Long Poll API; you need the community's number and a community access token.
channels-more.service.webex: Answers people who write to your Webex bot, and in spaces when the bot is mentioned; you need the bot's access token and a webhook secret you choose.
channels-more.service.x-dm: Answers X direct messages; needs your own X developer account on a paid API plan and a user access token.
channels-more.service.xmpp: Chat with the assistant from any XMPP (Jabber) app, one to one or in group rooms; you need an XMPP account for the assistant and its password.
channels-more.service.zalo: Answers people who message your Zalo Official Account; you need the app id, the app secret, the OA secret key and an access token with its refresh token.

documents.intro.your-own-documents-kept-: Your own documents, kept on this computer so the assistant can quote them. Word files, spreadsheets, slide decks, OpenDocument files, e-books, rich text, web pages, notes, tables, plain text and PDFs are all read here. A PDF that is pictures of text has no words to lift out, and says so.
documents.note.a-filter-that-matches-not: A filter narrows the search before anything is ranked, and two filters narrow it further. If nothing matches, Branch says so rather than answering from everything else you have.
documents.note.naming-project-files-is-o: This is off unless you want it. Most questions are not about code, and a list of file names in front of every question would only get in the way. When it is on, it speaks last: a knowledge base or a document of yours is always preferred.
documents.note.vectors-are-kept-in-branc: Matching by meaning needs a list of numbers for every passage. They are kept in the database Branch already has. If you have a large library you can put them in a database file of your own instead, on any drive. Nothing is deleted by changing this: press Read it again to fill the new place.

never-break.lead: A small gatekeeper keeps Branch's address open and starts the assistant again if it stops. Interrupted work carries on where it left off, and a new version is tried on a copy of your work before it is used.
never-break.mode.off: Branch runs as it always has: if it stops, it stays stopped until it is opened again.
never-break.mode.on: The gatekeeper starts Branch again if it stops, and interrupted work carries on by itself. It still asks you about any step that may already have reached someone else.
never-break.mode.when-needed: The gatekeeper starts Branch again if it stops, and asks you before carrying on interrupted work.
never-break.next-start: Branch can never change these settings, its own program, or your saved work by itself. It can only suggest a change here.
never-break.now.next-start: The gatekeeper will be used from the next time Branch starts.
never-break.now.off: Right now: Branch runs without the gatekeeper.
never-break.now.restarting: Right now: the assistant is being started again. It has been started again {count} times since the gatekeeper started.
never-break.now.running: Right now: the gatekeeper is running and the assistant is up. It has been started again {count} times since the gatekeeper started.
never-break.proposal.title: A suggested change is waiting for you
never-break.proposal.tried-bad: It did not start cleanly when it was tried, so it cannot be used.
never-break.proposal.tried-ok: It was tried on a throwaway copy and started cleanly.
never-break.saved: Saved. This takes effect the next time Branch starts.
obsidian.intro: Branch can write what it remembers, what it has learned and the reports you save into a folder of Markdown notes — the kind of folder Obsidian keeps. It never writes over a note you have edited yourself: the new version goes beside it instead. It reads back only the notes you have tagged #branch. Nothing is installed into Obsidian.

reviewer.lead: Another model looks at a risky step before you are asked about it: it says whether a tool only reads, and it can hold back a step that goes against your rules.
reviewer.modes: When needed looks only at tools that do not say what they do and at commands none of your rules decide about. On also looks at every step that would wait for your yes, and at every command.
reviewer.promise: It can only make things stricter. A step it holds back comes to you with its reason, and you can still allow it that once. If it cannot answer, your rules decide on their own. Each look costs what any other model call costs.
reviewer.stock-rules: Left empty, these are used: refuse anything that sends your files, passwords or keys where the task did not ask, deletes things outside the task's folder, downloads a program and runs it, hides what it does, or reaches for more access than it needs. Ask about spending money, messaging someone, publishing, or anything that cannot be undone.

settings.file.off: Not read. Turn it on above.
settings.file.permission-shaped: {count} of these lines ask for permission. Your assistant still reads them, but permission comes from your approval rules and nothing written in a file can change that.
settings.intro.keychain: Branch reads a password only for an entry listed here, and only when a task needs it. This list holds names, never passwords.
settings.intro.make-this-workspace-feel-: Make this workspace feel like yours.
settings.intro.screen-switch: Off to start with. When needed, the screen tools are fetched only when a task calls for them; on, they come with every task.
settings.intro.speech-engines: Write speech out or read replies aloud with Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Azure, or a program on this computer such as Piper. Keys stay in Secrets; you only name them here.
settings.intro.system-voice: Off to start with. Reads replies aloud with the voices already on this computer, free and offline.
settings.intro.video-programs: Uses ffmpeg and yt-dlp, if they are already on this computer, to look at still pictures from a video, write out what is said in it, and save videos or their captions from the web. Branch never installs them.
settings.intro.what-this-computer-allows: This computer has switches of its own. Branch never changes them; here is what each one is for.
settings.learning-core.confirm: Forget everything Branch has learned from experience? This cannot be undone.
settings.learning-core.draft-opened: A draft skill from the steps that kept working is open below. Read it, change it, and install it if you want it.
settings.learning-core.empty: Nothing learned yet. Turn it on and work as usual; habits appear here after a few tasks.
settings.learning-core.forgotten: Forgotten. It starts again from nothing.
settings.learning-core.kept: It keeps what it learned about {count} tools, skills and notes, on this computer only.
settings.learning-core.saved: Saved. It applies from your next task.
settings.note.agents-file: A file in the project folder saying how you want work done here. Written after something goes the wrong way, it changes the next task rather than the one after you remember to mention it.
settings.note.files-cannot-grant: A file can change how your assistant works and how it talks to you. It cannot give it permission it does not already have — your approval rules decide that, every time a tool runs.
settings.note.heartbeat-file: A list your assistant reads each time it wakes on a schedule. An empty file means there is nothing to do and it goes back to sleep without spending anything.
settings.note.learning-core: Branch notices which tools, skills and notes helped in tasks like yours, and which did not. It asks no model to do this and keeps no words from your requests.
settings.note.learning-core-forget: Forgetting clears only what this has learned. Your notes, skills and conversations stay as they are.
settings.note.learning-core-modes: Off: nothing is learned. Only when it is needed: it learns, and your assistant asks it when the work calls for it. On: it also chooses what to try first at the start of every task.
settings.note.memory-file: Everything else here your assistant remembered on its own. This is a file you write, so you can open it, read the whole thing and change your mind about any of it.
settings.note.persona-files: Write these in plain words and your assistant reads them before it does anything else. What you put in the first one replaces its built-in character rather than being added to it.
settings.note.security-audit-mode: Off: only when you press the button. Only when it is needed: your assistant can also run the check when you ask it whether your setup is safe. On: it also runs each time Branch starts.
settings.note.security-check: Looks over how Branch is set up on this computer — who else can read its files, who can reach it, and what it may do without asking — and puts right what it can.
settings.note.security-fix: Fixing only ever takes other people’s access away from Branch’s own files. Everything else needs a decision from you, so it is described instead.
settings.note.security-malware-mode: Before a server fetched with npx, uvx or pipx starts, its name is looked up in the public list of harmful packages (OSV), and a listed one is refused.
settings.note.sop-file: Steps you want followed the same way every time, written as prose rather than built as a procedure.
settings.note.tools-file: What your assistant should know about the programs on this computer: which one to reach for, and the quirks it would otherwise find out the hard way.
settings.nothing: No setting says that. Try another word.
settings.second-opinion.debate-intro: For a question worth the cost, two connections answer on their own and then read each other. It stops at whichever of these two it reaches first, and says which one stopped it.
settings.second-opinion.intro: Have another connection read a finished answer and say whether it stands up. It is shown beside the answer and never written into it, so you read both. Off until you turn it on, and it costs what any other model call costs.
settings.second-opinion.same-connection-: Leaving this on the one that answered is a weaker check: a model rarely argues with itself.
settings.security.not-checked: Not checked yet. Press Run the check.
settings.title: Settings
skills.card.share-a-skill-or-open: Share a skill, or open one someone sent you
skills.empty.none-written-next: Switch writing new skills on, then ask for one from a conversation.
skills.intro.a-skill-is-a-page: A skill is a page of written instructions your assistant can follow — how you like a letter laid out, the steps for a monthly report. It knows the name of every skill you keep here, and reads the one it needs. A skill never grants permission to do anything; your rules still decide that.
skills.note.skills-your-assistant-wrote: Your assistant can write a new skill from something that went well. Each one arrives switched off, is tried on past tasks with and without it, and waits here for your yes.
skills.note.skip-trial: Trying a new skill is how you find out it does not make tasks go worse. Keeping it without that means nobody has checked.
skills.note.writing-positions: Only when it is needed: only when you ask, by typing /learn in a conversation or with the box below. On: also after a task that looked like steps worth keeping.
specialists.intro.assistants-that-do-one: Assistants that do one job and are allowed to touch only what that job needs — the one that tidies your invoices cannot open your photographs. A new one has to pass the checks written into it before you can switch it on.
telegram-setup.lead: Talk to your assistant from Telegram on your phone. It takes about two minutes, and nothing is sent anywhere until you switch it on.
telegram-setup.now.nothing: No bot is set up yet.
telegram-setup.now.saved: A token is saved. The bot connects when Branch next starts with Telegram switched on.
telegram-setup.pair-lead: Pair your own account: send your bot a message, then type the six-digit code it sends back.
telegram-setup.paired: Paired. Your messages now reach the assistant.
telegram-setup.safety: Messages from Telegram can never run commands on this computer, and only people you have paired are answered.
telegram-setup.saved: Saved. Branch connects your bot the next time it starts.
telegram-setup.step-1: Open Telegram and search for BotFather (it has a blue tick). Start a chat with it.
telegram-setup.step-2: Send it the message /newbot, then choose a name for your assistant and a username that ends in "bot".
telegram-setup.step-3: BotFather replies with a long code called a token. Copy it and paste it below. Keep it to yourself: anyone with it can use your bot.
telegram-setup.step-4: Save, restart Branch, then send your bot any message. It answers with a six-digit code: type that code below to pair your account.
telegram-setup.token-kept: A token is saved; paste a new one only to replace it
telegram-setup.token-note: The token goes straight into Branch's locked store of secrets and is never shown on screen again.

terminal.keys.help1: Esc, then 1-5 (or Alt+1 to Alt+5): Conversation, Inbox, Automations, Library, Customize
terminal.keys.help2: Ctrl+K or /: find anything · Ctrl+N: new conversation · Ctrl+P or F2: side pane
terminal.keys.help3: In a place: up and down choose, left and right change tab, Enter opens, Tab asks
terminal.keys.help4: In Settings: left and right change page, Tab changes the Models tab, Esc closes
terminal.keys.help5: PgUp and PgDn scroll the conversation · Ctrl+L draws everything again
terminal.keys.line: Enter sends · Alt+Enter adds a line · Up recalls · Ctrl+E shows step details · Ctrl+C stops the task · Ctrl+D leaves

usage.intro: What your assistant has done this month, what it cost, and the limits you have set. Figures are worked out on this computer from your own tasks.
usage.report.lead: A page you can keep or hand on: what your assistant did and what it probably cost over a stretch of days, beside the same stretch before it.
usage.report.note: Made on this computer from its own records and sent nowhere. Costs are estimates from the prices on file, not a bill; keys are blanked out before the file is written.
usage.report.popup: Your browser would not open the print view. Allow pop-ups for this page.

developer.pull-requests.title: Pull requests from changes
developer.pull-requests.note: When this is on, a task that changed files can put them on a new branch, send it to GitHub with this computer's own Git sign-in and open a draft pull request. It never sends to a shared branch such as main, and a short-lived key can never use it. GitHub must be connected first.
developer.pull-requests.on: After every task that changed files

wsedit.card.title: Code editor
wsedit.card.note: Open and change text files in your workspace from the Files tab of a conversation. Every save can be put back, and a file that changed since you opened it is never overwritten.
